text:
Potent storms and flooding could disrupt the plans of tens of millions of people traveling for Thanksgiving, according to the US’s National Weather Service (NWS).
A storm system affecting the US Pacific north-west and another affecting the eastern part of the country are expected to produce periods of heavy rain and strong wind gusts, the NWS said as millions of Americans prepared to travel for Thursday’s holiday.
The NWS advised residents to check its website “for the latest forecast updates along your travel route and plan ahead”.
Both will bring the potential for periods of heavy rain and strong wind gusts.
Before Thanksgiving, parts of the US south are expected see heavy rain, including Florida, Georgia, the Carolinas, Alabama, Mississippi and Tennessee, according to the Weather Channel.
Parts of the midwestern states of Missouri, Illinois and Iowa are predicted to see rain – which could become wet snow, the outlet said. And, on Thanksgiving itself, midwest airports in Chicago, St Louis, Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and Detroit could see complications.
Meanwhile, seasonal high tides up and down California’s coast are expected to trigger “major to extreme” coastal flooding, with the San Francisco Bay Area particularly being advised to prepare for travel-related delays.
Furthermore, out west on Thanksgiving, there could be mountain snow in Washington and Oregon – and possibly into Idaho and Montana, according to the Weather Channel.
Inclement weather could affect up to 81 million people expected to travel throughout the US for Thanksgiving, widely reputed to be the busiest travel period in the US. The AAA motor club anticipates more than 72 million travelers will head for their holiday destinations by car, as NBC News reported.
Beside the weather, holiday car commuters will also be grappling with gasoline prices that have been particularly high in the wake of the war in Iran that the Trump administration started alongside Israel in February. AAA data showed regular gasoline averaged $3.64 a gallon in the US on Monday – six cents above a Thanksgiving Day record set in 2022, according to the motor club.
